bib.title: XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System
bib.venue: ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD)

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System", Tianqi Chen and Carlos Guestrin (University of Washington), KDD '16 (PDF is arXiv:1603.02754v3, 10 Jun 2016), 13 pages.

COVERAGE: 60,805 of 60,805 chars, all 13 pages, including Appendix A (pp. 11-13). Nothing skipped; references were read for origins. Quotes have PDF line breaks rejoined but keep end-of-line hyphens. I worked from text and captions and did not view the figure images, so figure curves were not checked.

CLAIMS

- claim: The sparsity-aware algorithm is about 50x faster than a naive version. This is a speed result only, with no accuracy comparison.
  number: 50x / "more than 50"
  setup: Allstate-10K, sparse mainly from one-hot encoding; 1 to 16 threads; time per tree. Complexity becomes linear in non-missing entries.
  quote: "We find that the sparsity aware algorithm runs 50 times faster than the naive version." Fig. 5 caption: "The sparsity aware algorithm is more than 50 times faster than the naive version"
  where: p5, Sec 3.4, offsets 21727 and 22118

- claim: XGBoost matches scikit-learn's AUC on exact greedy at over 10x the speed. R's gbm is faster than scikit-learn but far less accurate.
  number: time per tree / test AUC: XGBoost 0.6841 / 0.8304; colsample=0.5 0.6401 / 0.8245; scikit-learn 28.51 / 0.8302; R.gbm 1.032 / 0.6224
  setup: Higgs-1M (dense, chosen for fairness; subset so scikit-learn finishes); 500 trees, max depth 8, shrinkage 0.1; Dell PowerEdge R420, two eight-core Xeon E5-2470 2.3GHz, 64GB; all available cores unless specified. Table 1 lists scikit-learn and R GBM as not parallel, so this is probably parallel XGBoost against serial baselines (see LIMITS).
  quote: "Table 3: Comparison of Exact Greedy Methods with 500 trees on Higgs-1M data." / "XGBoost 0.6841 0.8304" / "scikit-learn 28.51 0.8302" / "XGBoost runs more than 10x faster than scikit-learn."
  where: p8, Sec 6.3, offsets 36980, 38697

- claim: Column subsampling's effect depends on the dataset. It lowered AUC slightly on Higgs but raised NDCG and cut time on Yahoo.
  number: Higgs AUC 0.8304 to 0.8245, 0.6841 to 0.6401 s/tree; Yahoo NDCG@10 0.7892 to 0.7913, 0.826 to 0.506 s/tree
  setup: Higgs-1M and Yahoo LTRC, 500 trees. The authors offer hedged explanations ("could due to") for both.
  quote: "XGBoost (colsample=0.5) 0.6401 0.8245" / "XGBoost (colsample=0.5) 0.506 0.7913" / "we also find column subsamples gives slightly worse performance than using all the features"
  where: p8, Tables 3 and 4; p9, Sec 6.4, offset 40163

- claim: On learning to rank XGBoost is about 3x faster than pGBRT (ratio is mine), but pGBRT has the highest NDCG, narrowly.
  number: XGBoost 0.826 s / 0.7892; colsample 0.506 s / 0.7913; pGBRT 2.576 s / 0.7915
  setup: Yahoo LTRC (473K rows, 700 features, official split), 500 trees; XGBoost exact greedy, pGBRT approximate only.
  quote: "pGBRT [22] 2.576 0.7915"
  where: p8, Table 4, offset 37350

- claim: The leaf weight and split gain have closed forms from second-order statistics, and setting regularisation to zero recovers traditional gradient tree boosting.
  number: Eq. 2 Omega = gamma T + 1/2 lambda ||w||^2; Eqs 5, 6, 7
  setup: Differentiable convex loss, second-order Taylor approximation, fixed tree structure, greedy split search.
  quote: "When the regularization parameter is set to zero, the objective falls back to the traditional gradient tree boosting."
  where: pp2-3, Sec 2.1-2.2

- claim: The authors credit the second-order method to Friedman et al. and call their objective changes minor.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 2 framing. Bears on the note's interview line listing second-order leaf weights among what XGBoost adds.
  quote: "Specicially the second order method is originated from Friedman et al. [12]. We make mi-nor improvements in the reguralized objective, which were found helpful in practice."
  where: p2, Sec 2, offset 7195

- claim: Missing values follow a default direction learnt at each node, by trying both directions while visiting only non-missing entries. Missing values, zeros and one-hot sparsity are handled in one way.
  number: none
  setup: Alg. 3; also applies to the approximate setting.
  quote: "The optimal default directions are learnt from the data." / "The key improvement is to only visit the non-missing entries"
  where: p5, Sec 3.4

- claim: Quantile-based approximate split finding can match exact greedy AUC, and local proposals need fewer candidates than global ones.
  number: eps=0.3 and 0.05, roughly 1/eps buckets
  setup: Higgs 10M, test AUC against iterations (Fig. 3). Caption legend: exact greedy, global eps=0.3, local eps=0.3, global eps=0.05. Results are shown only as a plot.
  quote: "This roughly translates to 1 / eps buckets in the proposal." / "the quantile strategy can get the same accuracy as exact greedy given reasonable approximation level."
  where: p4, Sec 3.2, offset 16776

- claim: The second-order statistic h_i acts as the instance weight in the split-proposal rank, because the objective can be rewritten as weighted squared loss. The paper introduces a weighted quantile sketch with a guarantee.
  number: merge error max(e1, e2); prune error e + 1/b
  setup: Eqs 8-9, Sec 3.3; Theorems A.1 and A.2.
  quote: "which is exactly weighted squared loss with labels gi/hi and weights hi." / "Then Q′(D) is a (ϵ + 1b )-approximate summary." (the extraction flattens 1/b to "1b")
  where: p4, Sec 3.3; p12 offset 57656; p13 offset 60342

- claim: Pre-sorted column blocks remove a log factor from exact greedy, and sorting need only be computed once.
  number: O(Kd||x||_0 log n) to O(Kd||x||_0 + ||x||_0 log n); approximate O(Kd||x||_0 log q) to O(Kd||x||_0 + ||x||_0 log B); q usually 32 to 100
  setup: K trees, depth d, ||x||_0 non-missing entries, B max rows per block. Analysis, not a measurement.
  quote: "tree boosting on the block structure only cost O(Kd‖x‖0 +‖x‖0 logn)." / "q is usually between 32 and 100"
  where: p6, Sec 4.1, offset 24789

- claim: Cache-aware prefetching doubles exact greedy speed on large data, and 2^16 rows per block balances cache use against parallelism.
  number: 2x; 2^16 examples per block
  setup: Allstate and Higgs; the effect appears at 10M rows (Figs 7, 9; block sizes tested 2^12 to 2^24).
  quote: "cache-aware implementation of the exact greedy algorithm runs twice as fast as the naive version when the dataset is large." / "choosing 2 16 examples per block balances the cache property and parallelization."
  where: p6, offset 27481; p7, offset 28554

- claim: Out-of-core compression and sharding each speed training, and one machine handled the full Criteo set.
  number: compression 3x, two-disk sharding a further 2x, 26% to 29% compression ratio, 1.7 billion examples; the basic method stops at 200M; file cache runs out from 400M
  setup: One AWS c3.8xlarge (32 vcores, two 320GB SSD, 60GB RAM); Criteo subsets; time per tree.
  quote: "compression helps to speed up computation by factor of three, and sharding into two disks further gives 2x speedup." / "Our final method is able to process 1.7 billion examples on a single machine." / "we achieve roughly a 26% to 29% compression ratio."
  where: p9, Sec 6.5, offsets 40613, 41103; p7, offset 30054

- claim: On a cluster XGBoost beats Spark MLLib and H2O per iteration and is the only one reaching the full data at this scale.
  number: over 10x Spark per iteration, 2.2x H2O; full 1.7B on as few as 4 machines
  setup: YARN on EC2, 32 m3.2xlarge (8 vcores, 30GB RAM, two 80GB SSD); 10 iterations; Criteo subsets; data on S3. H2O loads data slowly, so its end-to-end time is worse. Caption wording is garbled.
  quote: "XGBoost runs more 10x than spark per iteration and 2.2x as H2O's optimized version" / "XGBoost is able to handle the entire 1.7 billion data with only four machines."
  where: p9, Fig. 12 caption offset 42195; p9, Sec 6.6 offset 43525

- claim: XGBoost was widely used in 2015 competitions.
  number: 17 of 29 Kaggle winning solutions, 8 XGBoost alone, deep nets in 11; every top-10 KDDCup 2015 team
  setup: Solutions published on Kaggle's blog during 2015, from top-3 teams. Self-reported by the authors.
  quote: "Among the 29 challenge winning solutions 3 published at Kaggle's blog during 2015, 17 solutions used XGBoost." / "eight solely used XGBoost" / "was used in 11 solutions" / "XGBoost was used by every winning team in the top-10."
  where: p1, offsets 3240, 3583

- claim: Per user feedback, column subsampling prevents overfitting more than row subsampling. This is anecdotal, not measured here.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 2.3; the authors also state it speeds the parallel algorithm.
  quote: "According to user feedback, using column sub-sampling prevents over-fitting even more so than the traditional row sub-sampling"
  where: p3, offset 13061

- claim: A feature comparison of six systems records only XGBoost as having all of exact, approximate global and local, out-of-core, sparsity-aware and parallel.
  number: Table 1: scikit-learn exact yes, everything else no; R GBM exact yes, sparsity partial, not parallel; Spark MLLib and H2O approximate global, partial sparsity, parallel; pGBRT approximate local, parallel
  setup: The authors' own 2016 table.
  quote: "scikit-learn yes no no no no no"
  where: p7, offset 28210

- claim: Criteo ID features were replaced with count and average-CTR statistics computed on an earlier period rather than encoded directly.
  number: first ten days for statistics, next ten for training; 67 features
  setup: The authors say tree models handle continuous features better. Possibly useful beside the note's target-encoding section.
  quote: "calculating the statistics of average CTR and count of ID features on the first ten days, replacing the ID features by the corresponding count statistics during the next ten days for training."
  where: p8, Sec 6.2

LIMITS
- Thread confound: Sec 6.2 says experiments use all available cores, and Table 1 marks scikit-learn and R GBM non-parallel. Sec 6.3 does not state thread counts or isolate threading, so the "more than 10x" is not shown to be algorithmic. The Intro's "more than ten times faster than existing popular solutions on a single machine" is the general form of this claim.
- Sparsity result: speed only. No test of default directions against imputation, and no accuracy impact reported. It is measured on a 10K subset.
- No variance: all tables are single figures, with no seeds, spread or significance tests. Table 3's 0.8304 vs 0.8302 and Table 4's gaps cannot be separated from noise using this paper.
- Scaling experiments (Figs 11-13) report time only, not accuracy.
- Common settings (depth 8, shrinkage 0.1) with no per-system tuning. The authors say only "We can find similar results when we use other settings of maximum depth", with no data shown.
- Comparators are 2016 systems. LightGBM and CatBoost do not appear. The paper's approximate method is quantile-sketch proposals; it mentions histograms only as an alternative [22], and there is no `hist` tree method or native categorical handling (Criteo IDs were preprocessed by hand). Table 1 and the hardware are dated.
- The paper does not study regularisation's accuracy effect: lambda and gamma are never varied in an experiment. "Helpful in practice" is an unquantified assertion. Shrinkage is not varied either.
- The Kaggle evidence is usage counts, and the authors concede feature engineering plays "an important role". They also report ensembles beat a well-configured XGBoost "by only a small amount" [1], which is second-hand.
- Sec 6.6 says performance "scales linearly"; the Fig. 13 caption says "slightly super linear", attributed to more file cache.
- No interpretability, calibration or prediction-latency evaluation.

BUILDS ON
- Friedman 2001 [10] gradient boosting; Friedman 2002 [11] shrinkage (the paper credits this for shrinkage, under the title "Stochastic gradient boosting").
- Friedman, Hastie, Tibshirani 2000 [12] second-order method.
- Breiman 2001 [4] and Friedman and Popescu 2003 [13] column subsampling; TreeNet is noted as commercial precedent.
- Zhang and Johnson 2014 [25] regularized greedy forest, which the objective resembles but simplifies.
- Greenwald and Khanna 2001 [14] and Zhang and Wang 2007 [24] quantile summaries.
- Li et al. 2008 [17], Bekkerman et al. 2011 [2], Tyree et al. 2011 [22] approximate framework.
- Ye et al. 2009 [23] and Panda et al. 2009 [19] parallel trees.
- Burges 2010 [5] LambdaMART; Fan et al. 2008 [9] LIBLINEAR, for sparsity in linear models.

CODE: no runnable code; the paper has pseudocode only. Alg. 1 (exact greedy, p3) and Alg. 3 (sparsity-aware, p5). The extraction garbles them (e.g. "G2L HL+λ"), so re-type from the PDF. The missing-direction core of Alg. 3, verbatim:
"// enumerate missing value goto right
GL← 0, HL← 0
for j in sorted(Ik, ascent order by xjk ) do"
Alg. 1 initialises "gain← 0" but then updates "score", an inconsistency in the source. It also omits gamma from the score.

FIGURES (captions only; images not viewed)
- Fig. 2, p3, "Structure Score Calculation. We only need to sum up the gradient and second order gradient statistics on each leaf, then apply the scoring formula to get the quality score." Makes Eq. 6 concrete; pairs with the note's hand-check.
- Fig. 4, p4, "Tree structure with default directions. An example will be classified into the default direction when the feature needed for the split is missing." Shows the mechanism at a glance.
- Fig. 6, p5, "Block structure for parallel learning. Each column in a block is sorted by the corresponding feature value. A linear scan over one column in the block is sufficient to enumerate all the split points." Explains parallelism inside a tree, which the note states in prose.
- Fig. 3, p4, "Comparison of test AUC convergence on Higgs 10M dataset..." Shows approximate matching exact, and global vs local.
- Fig. 5, p5, "Impact of the sparsity aware algorithm on Allstate-10K..." Shows the 50x gap across thread counts.
- Fig. 1, p2, "Tree Ensemble Model. The final prediction for a given example is the sum of predictions from each tree." Possible for 06-ensembles.
- Fig. 11, p9 and Fig. 13, p10: out-of-core and machine scaling. Lower value for these notes.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction is sound overall, but equations and pseudocode are flattened, so check Eqs 5-7, the complexity formulas and exponents against the PDF. For example "2 16" is 2^16, and "1b" is 1/b.
- Source typos are preserved in quotes ("Specicially", "reguralized", "could due to", "runs more 10x than spark").
- Internal inconsistencies: "50 times" (body) vs "more than 50 times" (caption); "linearly" vs "super linear".
- Table 2 gives Higgs m=28 and Allstate n=10 M; Allstate-10K and Higgs-1M are subsets.
- No embedded instructions found.
- Against the notes, without judging: 07-boosting-in-practice.md lines 94 and 232 use the Higgs figures correctly, but line 232 reports only the Higgs direction of colsample, not the opposite Yahoo result. Line 274 lists second-order weights as an XGBoost addition, while the paper credits them to Friedman et al. Line 94's "more than 50 times" matches the caption. 06-ensembles.md does not cite this paper.
